claims.text: Covariance analysis of atomic displacements can be used to estimate vibrational entropy.
Eigenvalues of the atomic-displacement covariance matrix encode effective vibrational modes or frequencies.
The covariance matrix encapsulates short-scale ordering in the material.
A covariance-derived effective harmonic model can incorporate some anharmonicity through temperature-dependent effective vibrational frequencies.
Configuration ensembles rather than explicit time evolution are sufficient for the covariance-based entropy analysis.
Short trajectories alone will provide statistically representative ensembles for accurate entropy extraction.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials can supply the required short ensembles while preserving ab initio fidelity.
The Gaussian covariance approach should work best when atomic displacements are small or approximately Gaussian.
Accuracy may deteriorate when strong anharmonicity or non-Gaussian correlations dominate.
The covariance-based entropy method agrees well with experimental vibrational entropies for BCC sodium and FCC aluminum above their Debye temperatures.
The covariance-based method also agrees well with experiment for elemental sodium and aluminum down to low temperatures when its covariance eigenvalues are treated quantum mechanically.
The method has been applied to the MoNbTaW high-entropy alloy.
The demonstrated solid-state covariance method extends to liquid states near fusion.
Covariance-derived vibrational entropy captures the essential entropy contributions needed for both solid and fluid free energies.
The hybrid method will reproduce solid and liquid phase free energies, fusion temperatures, and related observables within about 5% of explicit AIMD or TOR-TILD results.
The hybrid method will reduce computational cost by roughly one to two orders of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD or TOR-TILD.
The covariance approach can retain the relevant electron-vibration coupling effects needed for faithful phase free energies.
Explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD free-energy workflows fully include vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron-vibration coupling but require extensive sampling.
